texts.orig: Understand the analytical thinking interview
texts.text: Understand the analytical thinking interview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Analytical thinking (AT) interviews assess a candidate’s ability to understand a product in the context of its broader company and its market, establish metrics to track success, identify team goals, and evaluate tradeoffs in a structured way. Here are some examples of typical AT questions:
texts.text: Analytical thinking (AT) interviews assess a candidate’s ability to understand a product in the context of its broader company and its market, establish metrics to track success, identify team goals, and evaluate tradeoffs in a structured way. Here are some examples of typical AT questions:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: “How would you measure success for Spotify?”
texts.text: “How would you measure success for Spotify?”

texts.text: “You’re a PM at Meta. Set a goal for Instagram Reels.”

texts.text: “What should be the North Star metric for DoorDash?”

texts.orig: Although an AT interview normally lasts 45 minutes, you’ll have only about 35 minutes of actual working time after accounting for introductions and wrap-up questions. That might seem like plenty of time, but it flies by, so you’ll want to let your inner “time cop” run the show.

texts.text: Step 1: Assumptions and game plan

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The opening minutes of an analytical thinking interview can make or break your performance. I’ve watched countless candidates struggle because they jumped straight into goals without aligning with the interviewer on the structure.
texts.text: The opening minutes of an analytical thinking interview can make or break your performance. I’ve watched countless candidates struggle because they jumped straight into goals without aligning with the interviewer on the structure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My advice is to approach the interview as a game with clear rules rather than a casual conversation, and spend the first minute making a handful of assumptions at the start of the interview that narrow the scope to a manageable exercise without prematurely limiting the solution space. Then outline your game plan for the interview, showing the interviewer how you want to spend your time together.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you can’t describe your metric to a data scientist in a way that they could run a query with, it’s not a useful metric. Always define metrics so specifically that someone could implement them tomorrow, and focus on 3-5 primary metrics per ecosystem player rather than trying to capture everything. Metric selection can also become problematic if you use averages or ratios as North Star metrics. Here’s why this backfires: if your NSM increases while your ecosystem actually shrinks, you’re getting a false positive. I’ve watched candidates confidently present metrics that could look great even as their product dies (not exactly what you want to signal to an interviewer).

texts.orig: Debugging questions
texts.text: Debugging questions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Debugging questions (also known as “root cause” analysis) assess your ability to systematically diagnose problems and identify potential causes. These questions typically present a scenario where some metric has moved and you need to determine what happened. Although debugging questions are becoming less common (particularly at Meta), they still occasionally appear to assess analytical skills.
texts.text: Debugging questions (also known as “root cause” analysis) assess your ability to systematically diagnose problems and identify potential causes. These questions typically present a scenario where some metric has moved and you need to determine what happened. Although debugging questions are becoming less common (particularly at Meta), they still occasionally appear to assess analytical skills.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Here’s an example:
texts.text: Here’s an example:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “You’re a PM at DoorDash and noticed orders were down 10% last week. What happened?”
texts.text: “You’re a PM at DoorDash and noticed orders were down 10% last week. What happened?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To approach this, you’ll start by clarifying the observed issue: restate the scenario to ensure understanding, including the magnitude of the metric movement and the time frame in which it’s been observed.
texts.text: To approach this, you’ll start by clarifying the observed issue: restate the scenario to ensure understanding, including the magnitude of the metric movement and the time frame in which it’s been observed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Then you’ll want to break down key dimensions like geos/markets, platforms, and segments to identify where exactly the anomalous behavior might have originated and for which users.
texts.text: Then you’ll want to break down key dimensions like geos/markets, platforms, and segments to identify where exactly the anomalous behavior might have originated and for which users.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This will allow you to generate hypotheses for potential causes across technical issues, product changes, user behavior shifts, external factors, data issues, etc. Explicitly state each hypothesis before explaining how you’d test it.
texts.text: This will allow you to generate hypotheses for potential causes across technical issues, product changes, user behavior shifts, external factors, data issues, etc. Explicitly state each hypothesis before explaining how you’d test it.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The most common mistake I’ve seen here is candidates fixating on a single hypothesis and failing to generate multiple potential explanations for the observed issue. Don’t explore complex theories if simpler causes can explain what’s going on.
texts.text: The most common mistake I’ve seen here is candidates fixating on a single hypothesis and failing to generate multiple potential explanations for the observed issue. Don’t explore complex theories if simpler causes can explain what’s going on.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Estimation questions
texts.text: Estimation questions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Estimation questions, which historically are popular at Google, assess your ability to “ballpark” with limited information. These questions aren’t about arriving at the precise answer but, rather, demonstrating a logical approach to breaking down complex problems and reaching an answer within a reasonable order of magnitude.
texts.text: Estimation questions, which historically are popular at Google, assess your ability to “ballpark” with limited information. These questions aren’t about arriving at the precise answer but, rather, demonstrating a logical approach to breaking down complex problems and reaching an answer within a reasonable order of magnitude.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Here’s an example:
texts.text: Here’s an example:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “How many shuttle buses does Google need to transport employees from San Francisco to Mountain View each day?”
texts.text: “How many shuttle buses does Google need to transport employees from San Francisco to Mountain View each day?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To approach this, you’ll want to start by restating the question, ensuring that you understand what you’re being asked to estimate.
texts.text: To approach this, you’ll want to start by restating the question, ensuring that you understand what you’re being asked to estimate.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Next, you’ll want to break down the question by creating a logical formula that isolates all of the necessary components for reaching an answer. You’ll then plug reasonable assumptions into that formula, relying on personal experience and common knowledge as reference points (use round numbers in the right order of magnitude for simplicity). Remember to include all critical components; otherwise your estimates will be fundamentally flawed.
texts.text: Next, you’ll want to break down the question by creating a logical formula that isolates all of the necessary components for reaching an answer. You’ll then plug reasonable assumptions into that formula, relying on personal experience and common knowledge as reference points (use round numbers in the right order of magnitude for simplicity). Remember to include all critical components; otherwise your estimates will be fundamentally flawed.
